notes.21.25: 22.24 an dem ende read as 'on the forehead'. 23.3 verheret: 'despoiled', perhaps 'stripped of his host'. 23.11 Pitavium: Patavium, Padua. 23.13 Walhelant, 'land of the Romance-speakers', here Italy. 23.21 Xande in the text: the Trojan river Xanthus, matching the name of Xanten on the Rhine.

nodes.text: then hear about the fierce heathendom
from which the old cities got their strength.
Ninus was the name of the first man
who ever began warfare.
He gathered shield and spear;
he was very eager for glory.
He named the city Nineveh after himself,
where later the sea-fish spat out Jonah.
His wife was called Semiramis;
she founded old Babylon
from the old bricks
which the giants had fired
when Nimrod the great
foolishly advised them
However they set about their affairs,
they all had to serve the Romans.
Caesar began to draw near
to his own old kinsmen,
to the noble Franks.
The forefathers of both of them
came from old Troy,
when the Greeks laid the city low,
when over both the armies
God made his judgement so plain
that some of the Trojans escaped
and the Greeks dared not seek their homes,
for in the ten years
that they had been encamped there,
all their wives at home had married again;
they plotted against their husbands' lives.
Because of this King Agamemnon was slain.
The others wandered astray,
until the companions of Ulysses
were devoured by the Cyclops in Sicily,
which Ulysses well avenged with spears
when he put out his eye as he slept.
The race of the Cyclopes
was still at that time in Sicily,
as tall as pine trees;
on the forehead they had one eye.
Now God has driven them away from us, out of these parts,
into the wilderness beyond India.
The Trojans travelled through the world,
wandering far in search of a home,
until Helenus, a despoiled man,
took the widow of bold Hector,
with whom [he] there in Greece
occupied the realm of his enemies.
They built a Troy there
which could long be seen afterwards.
Antenor had gone away from there earlier,
when he saw that Troy was going to fall.
He founded for us the city of Patavium
by the river Timavus.
Aeneas won Italy for himself by fighting,
where he found the sow with thirty young.
There they built the city of Alba,
from which Rome was later founded.
Franko settled with his people
very far downstream by the Rhine.
There they joyfully built
a little Troy.
They called the stream Xanthus
after the river in their [own] land;
they took the Rhine for the sea.
From there the Frankish hosts later grew.
They all became subject to Caesar,
yet they were a cause of care to him.
When Caesar then went back to Rome,
they would not receive him.
